instruction: Replace every occurrence of localhost with 127.0.0.1 in config.ini, editing the file in place.
context: GNU sed: -i edits in place and its backup suffix is optional and attached, as in -i.bak. Supplying a separate empty argument the way BSD sed requires would make GNU sed treat '' as the script.

instruction: Replace every occurrence of localhost with 127.0.0.1 in config.ini in place on macOS.
context: BSD sed: -i requires an explicit backup-suffix argument, so an empty '' means no backup. Omitting it makes BSD sed consume the script as the suffix and then fail. This is the single most common macOS sed error.

instruction: Collapse runs of spaces into one using extended regular expressions, portably.
context: sed: -E enables extended regular expressions on both GNU and BSD. GNU also accepts -r as a synonym, but BSD does not, so -E is the portable spelling to prefer in shared scripts.

instruction: Print the date seven days ago in ISO format.
context: GNU date: -d parses a free-form date description including relative phrases. BSD date has no -d; it uses -v with adjustment units instead.

instruction: Print the date seven days ago in ISO format on macOS.
context: BSD date: -v adjusts the date by a signed amount and a unit letter, so -v-7d means seven days earlier. The adjustment attaches directly to -v with no space. GNU's -d '7 days ago' is not accepted.

instruction: Convert the Unix timestamp 1700000000 to a readable UTC time.
context: GNU date: prefixing a number with @ inside -d interprets it as seconds since the Unix epoch, and -u renders the result in UTC. BSD date spells this as -r with a bare number.

instruction: Convert the Unix timestamp 1700000000 to a readable UTC time on macOS.
context: BSD date: -r takes seconds since the epoch directly, with no @ prefix. On GNU date, -r instead means 'use this file's modification time', so the same flag has an entirely different meaning across platforms.

instruction: Print just the byte size of release.tar.gz.
context: GNU stat: -c takes a printf-style format where %s is the size in bytes. BSD stat uses -f for the format string and spells size as %z, so neither the flag nor the specifier carries over.

instruction: Print just the byte size of release.tar.gz on macOS.
context: BSD stat: -f supplies the format and %z is the byte size. GNU's -c %s means the same thing but neither spelling is accepted by the other implementation.

instruction: Show the octal permission bits of id_rsa.
context: GNU stat: %a renders the access rights in octal, which is how you confirm a key is 600. The BSD equivalent is stat -f %Lp.

instruction: Show the octal permission bits of id_rsa on macOS.
context: BSD stat: %p is the mode and the L modifier strips the file-type bits, leaving the permission digits alone. Without L the output includes the leading file-type code.

instruction: Decode a base64 payload stored in token.b64.
context: GNU coreutils base64: lowercase -d decodes. macOS spells the same operation with capital -D, and passing -d there is an error, which makes this one of the sharpest case splits between the platforms.

instruction: Decode a base64 payload stored in token.b64 on macOS.
context: macOS base64: capital -D decodes and -i names the input file. GNU's lowercase -d is rejected. Scripts that must run on both platforms usually shell out to openssl base64 -d instead.

instruction: Compute the SHA-256 checksum of release.tar.gz.
context: GNU coreutils provides sha256sum, md5sum, and friends as separate binaries. macOS ships none of them; it provides shasum with an algorithm flag and a separate md5 command.

instruction: Compute the SHA-256 checksum of release.tar.gz on macOS.
context: macOS: shasum -a selects the digest length, so -a 256 matches GNU sha256sum. The output format is compatible, so shasum -a 256 -c also verifies a checksum file written on Linux.

instruction: Get the MD5 hash of an ISO image to compare against a published value.
context: GNU coreutils: md5sum prints the hash followed by two spaces and the filename. macOS instead has a command literally named md5 whose default output is a single-line 'MD5 (file) = hash' form.

instruction: Get the MD5 hash of an ISO image on macOS printing only the hash.
context: macOS md5: -q is quiet mode and prints the bare hash with no filename wrapper, which makes it comparable to GNU md5sum output after cutting the first field.

instruction: Resolve a path to its fully canonical absolute form, following every symlink.
context: GNU coreutils: readlink -f canonicalizes the whole path and requires all but the last component to exist. Classic BSD readlink has no -f at all, which is why portable scripts reach for realpath or greadlink.

instruction: Resolve a path to its canonical absolute form on macOS.
context: macOS: realpath ships in recent releases and canonicalizes without needing a flag. On older systems neither realpath nor readlink -f exists, and the usual fallback is greadlink -f from Homebrew coreutils.

instruction: List every regular file under the tree with its size in bytes, largest first.
context: GNU find: -printf formats each result, where %s is the size in bytes and %p is the path. BSD find has no -printf at all, so on macOS the same job needs -exec stat -f '%z %N' {} +.

instruction: List every regular file under the tree with its size in bytes on macOS, largest first.
context: BSD find lacks -printf, so formatting is delegated to stat -f. The trailing + batches many paths into one stat invocation, which is far faster than the semicolon form that runs stat once per file.

instruction: Delete matching files but do nothing at all when the search finds nothing.
context: GNU xargs: without -r, xargs runs the command once even when its input is empty, so 'rm' would execute with no operands. -r is a GNU extension; BSD xargs already skips empty input and does not accept it on older releases.

instruction: Delete matching files on macOS without erroring when nothing matches.
context: BSD xargs does not run the command when its input is empty, so the GNU -r flag is unnecessary here and is rejected by older macOS versions. The -0 and -print0 pairing still matters for filenames with spaces.

instruction: List files with colored output.
context: GNU ls: --color=auto colorizes only when stdout is a terminal, which keeps pipes clean. BSD ls on macOS has no --color long option and spells this as -G instead.

instruction: List files with colored output on macOS.
context: BSD ls: -G enables colorized output. There is no --color long option, and unlike GNU's auto mode this does not detect whether stdout is a pipe, so CLICOLOR_FORCE and pipes need care.

instruction: Find lines containing a word followed by a digit using a lookahead.
context: GNU grep: -P selects the PCRE engine, which is what enables lookarounds, \d, and \b. BSD grep on macOS has no -P, so ripgrep or perl is the usual substitute there.

instruction: Find out how many CPU cores are available for a parallel build.
context: GNU coreutils: nproc reports the number of processing units available to the current process, honoring CPU affinity and cgroup limits. macOS has no nproc and uses sysctl -n hw.ncpu.

instruction: Find out how many CPU cores are available on macOS.
context: macOS: sysctl -n prints a kernel state value without its name, and hw.ncpu is the logical core count. hw.physicalcpu excludes hyperthreads. There is no nproc in the base system.

instruction: Print the lines of a log file in reverse order, last line first.
context: GNU coreutils: tac is cat spelled backwards and reverses line order. macOS has no tac; the BSD equivalent is tail -r, which reverses its input.

instruction: Print the lines of a log file in reverse order on macOS.
context: BSD tail: -r prints lines in reverse order, filling the role of GNU tac. GNU tail has no -r, so this is a genuinely one-way substitution.

instruction: Rank the ten largest subdirectories of the current tree by size.
context: GNU sort: -h compares human-readable numbers so 2G outranks 900M, and -r reverses to descending. BSD sort on macOS has no -h, so the portable approach is du -sk with a plain numeric sort.

instruction: Rank the ten largest subdirectories by size on macOS.
context: macOS sort lacks GNU's -h, so du -sk emits a uniform kilobyte count that plain numeric -n can rank correctly. Mixing du -sh with sort -n instead compares the leading digits and puts 900M above 2G.

instruction: Find which process is listening on TCP port 8080.
context: iproute2 ss: -l shows listening sockets, -t restricts to TCP, -n keeps ports numeric, and -p attaches the owning process, which needs root to show other users. ss replaced netstat on modern Linux; macOS has neither and uses lsof.

instruction: Find which process is listening on TCP port 8080 on macOS.
context: macOS: lsof -i selects internet sockets and -sTCP:LISTEN narrows to listeners. -n skips DNS resolution and -P skips port-name lookup, which makes the output both faster and easier to grep. There is no ss on macOS.

instruction: Check how much memory is actually available.
context: procps free: -h formats with unit suffixes. The 'available' column matters more than 'free' because Linux counts reclaimable page cache as used. macOS has no free command and reports memory through vm_stat.

instruction: Check memory pressure statistics on macOS.
context: macOS: vm_stat reports Mach virtual memory counters in pages rather than bytes, so multiply by the page size it prints in the header. There is no free command in the base system.

instruction: Create a temporary working directory safely.
context: GNU mktemp: -d makes a directory instead of a file and prints its path. Calling it with no template is portable across GNU and BSD; supplying a bare template without trailing X characters is not.

instruction: Create a temporary directory with a recognizable name prefix on macOS.
context: BSD mktemp: -t takes a bare prefix and appends its own randomness under TMPDIR. GNU mktemp's -t is deprecated and instead expects a full template containing XXXXXX, so this spelling is not portable in reverse.

instruction: Run a health check but give up after five seconds.
context: GNU coreutils: timeout sends TERM after the duration and exits 124 when it fires. --kill-after adds a follow-up KILL. macOS has no timeout in the base system; Homebrew coreutils installs it as gtimeout.

instruction: Extract the shell field from every line of /etc/passwd.
context: cut: -d sets a single-character delimiter and -f selects fields by number. cut cannot treat runs of whitespace as one separator, which is why awk is the usual choice for column output that is space-aligned.

instruction: Show only the process ID and command name columns from a process listing.
context: awk: the default field separator collapses runs of whitespace, so $1 and $2 work on ragged column output where cut -f would not. NR > 1 skips the header line.
